intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains why a slide matters, how to remember it and where practice goes wrong. Work the examples with a pencil, check yourself against the questions, and note which sources and dates you must verify before quoting them.

sections.title: What mental health is, and what a disorder is
sections.big_idea: Mental health is **well-being that everyone has to some degree**, and the term you choose for a condition decides who your programme is built for.
in_plain_words: WHO describes mental health as a state of well-being that lets people cope with stress, realise their abilities, learn and work well and contribute to their community. It has value in itself and also makes learning, work and caregiving possible. That wide definition means a livelihood or education project can protect mental health even if it never treats anyone.

Three terms overlap. A mental disorder meets diagnostic criteria, a mental health condition also covers distress and disability that may never be diagnosed, and psychosocial disability describes the barriers society puts in a person's way. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 adds a legal definition in section 2(1)(s). **The person decides about their own care**, and your words in reports should put the person before the diagnosis.

children.label: Psychosocial disability
items: Can be reduced by a programme

diagram.caption: match the term to the activity

key_terms.meaning: State of well-being enabling coping, learning, working and contributing (WHO).
Clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion regulation or behaviour.
The barriers a person with a long-term condition meets in society.
WHO's coding system, effective for health reporting from January 2022.
Act 10 of 2017, in force from 29 May 2018, that presumes capacity.

worked_example.title: Choose the right term
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: you are writing three indicators for a programme. Pick the term that fits each activity, using the deck's rule.
steps: A household screening survey estimates how many people meet diagnostic criteria, so it counts disorders.
A village group programme works with distress and daily functioning, so it should say mental health condition or distress.
A project that removes barriers to school, work or voting works on psychosocial disability.
In all three, write 'a person living with' the condition and name the term in your indicators.
worked_example.answer: Survey: disorder. Community programme: distress and functioning. Barrier-removal: psychosocial disability.

mistakes: Defining mental health as the absence of illness. WHO describes a positive state that people with a diagnosis can also have.
Using 'committed suicide' or 'a schizophrenic' in reports. Use 'died by suicide' and 'a person living with schizophrenia'.
Treating a decision others disagree with as proof of incapacity. Section 4(3) says it is not.
Attempting to diagnose. Programme staff read ICD-coded notes and records and leave diagnosis to clinicians.

recall.q: What does WHO's definition start from?
recall.a: A state of mental well-being that enables people to cope with stress, realise their abilities, learn and work well and contribute to their community.

recall.q: Which of the three terms is narrowest?
recall.a: A mental disorder, which meets diagnostic criteria.

recall.q: When did the MHCA 2017 come into force?
recall.a: 29 May 2018. It received assent on 7 April 2017.

recall.q: Which section of the Act presumes capacity?
recall.a: Section 4.

recall.q: Give one word to avoid and its replacement.
recall.a: 'Committed suicide' becomes 'died by suicide', or 'suffering from' becomes 'living with'.

sections.title: How large the burden is
sections.big_idea: More than a billion people live with a mental health condition, and **most never receive effective care** even though effective treatment exists.
in_plain_words: Globally, 1.2 billion people lived with a mental disorder in 2023. In India the GBD estimate for 2017 was 197.3 million, and the National Mental Health Survey 2015-16 found 10.6% of adults with a current disorder. These two sources answer different questions. GBD is a modelled estimate for all India, while the survey covered 12 states with structured interviews.

The gap between need and care is the central problem. In India between 70% and 92% received no treatment, depending on the condition, and 85% for common disorders. Public services provided most of the care that was given. As of October 2026 the second national survey has no published report, so **state the year and coverage of any national number you quote**.

left.title: High-income countries
items: About 70% of people with psychosis treated
Only a third with depression get formal care

right.title: Low-income countries
items: Gap widest where incomes are lowest

diagram.caption: the care gap by income level

key_terms.meaning: Share of people with a condition who received no treatment.
Global Burden of Disease method: modelled estimates used for scale and comparison.
Disability-adjusted life year. Mental disorders mostly add years lived with disability.
India's first national survey of mental disorders, by NIMHANS in 12 states.
WHO's programme for mental, neurological and substance use disorders in primary care.

worked_example.title: Add the burden and the gap
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's own figures. First add India's DALY shares, then measure the care gap.
steps: Depressive and anxiety disorders: 33.8 + 19.0 = 52.8 per cent of mental disorder DALYs, so over half.
Add schizophrenia and bipolar disorder at 16.7: 52.8 + 16.7 = 69.5 per cent.
Care gap in psychosis: 70 − 12 = 58 percentage points between high-income and low-income countries.
Quote each with its source and year.
worked_example.answer: 52.8% for depression and anxiety, 69.5% with the severe disorders, and a 58-point gap in psychosis care.

mistakes: Putting the GBD 197 million and the NMHS 10.6% in one sentence as if they agree. They answer different questions.
Comparing a new survey figure with 10.6% before checking that it used the same tools.
Reading coverage as quality. A person may see a doctor once, take a prescription and never return.
Quoting NMHS-2 numbers when none had been published as of October 2026.

recall.q: How many people lived with a mental disorder globally in 2023?
recall.a: 1.2 billion, nearly 1 in 7 (WHO).

recall.q: How many Indians had a mental disorder in 2017 by GBD?
recall.a: 197.3 million, with 45.7 million depressive and 44.9 million anxiety disorders.

recall.q: What share of adults had a current disorder in NMHS 2015-16?
What was the treatment gap for common mental disorders in India?
What went to stand-alone psychiatric hospitals globally?
recall.a: Two out of every three dollars of government spending on mental health.

sections.title: Suicide: what the numbers show and what they miss
sections.big_idea: The recorded figure is a **floor**, and prevention works best on means, media, young people and follow-up.
in_plain_words: WHO counts 727,000 deaths by suicide worldwide in 2021. NCRB recorded 1,70,746 in India in 2024, a rate of 12.2 per lakh. Daily wage earners were nearly a third, and housewives were 48.9% of the women who died. NCRB's cause categories record the trigger an officer noted, a narrow view of a decision with many causes.

Police-recorded data under-counts. Families may report an accident, rural deaths go uncertified and states differ in how thoroughly they compile records. Use the number as a floor, compare trends within a state and avoid ranking. For prevention, WHO names four interventions. In Sri Lanka, **limiting access to the most toxic pesticides coincided with 19,769 fewer suicides** over ten years.

diagram.caption: five habits for reading recorded suicides

key_terms.meaning: NCRB's Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India, from police records.
Suicides per 100,000 population: 12.2 in India in 2024.
Deaths kept out of police records, so the true figure is higher.
Limiting access to the most toxic means, which gives a crisis time to pass.
Reporting that avoids method, location and single-cause stories.

worked_example.title: Check the figures behind two claims
worked_example.setup: A report says housewives were nearly half of women who died, and farming accounted for 10,546 deaths. Check both against NCRB 2024 as the deck gives it.
steps: So 'nearly half of women who died' is correct, and applies to women only.
Farming: 4,633 + 5,913 = 10,546 (cultivators plus agricultural labourers).
Share of all suicides: 10,546 ÷ 1,70,746 = 6.2%.
worked_example.answer: Both claims hold: 48.9% of women's deaths were housewives, and the farming sector was 6.2% of all suicides.

mistakes: Explaining any death by one cause, in conversation or in a report. WHO says suicidal behaviour is never the result of a single factor.
Ranking states by recorded suicides. The gaps partly reflect how well police record deaths.
Describing the method or naming the location in a programme newsletter.
Calling an attempt 'successful' or 'failed'. Say 'suicide attempt'.

recall.q: How many suicides did NCRB record in 2024 and at what rate?
recall.a: 1,70,746, a rate of 12.2 per lakh.

recall.q: Which source of under-count applies to rural deaths?
recall.a: They are certified without a medical cause.

recall.q: Name two of WHO's four LIVE LIFE interventions.
recall.a: Limit access to the means, work with media on responsible reporting, build socio-emotional life skills in adolescents, and follow up anyone affected by suicidal behaviour.

recall.q: Is asking directly about suicidal thoughts safe?
recall.a: Yes. WHO's fact says talking openly can give a person other options or time to rethink.

recall.q: Which helpline is free and round the clock in India?

sections.title: Social determinants: poverty, debt, caste, gender and stigma
sections.big_idea: Mental health is shaped by money, work, discrimination and stigma, so **programmes outside the health sector already touch it**.
in_plain_words: Poverty and common mental disorders feed each other. Insecurity, risk of violence and ill-health push poor people toward illness, and the costs of illness add lost work, spending on care and debt. Across 115 studies, education, food insecurity, housing, social class and financial stress were consistently linked, while income and employment were equivocal. A late cash transfer may do less than a smaller one on time.

Caste, gender and stigma add their own weight. Scheduled Castes and Muslims reported worse mental health than higher-caste Hindus, and status differences did not fully explain it. Depression is about 1.5 times more common among women. Stigma, described by many as worse than the condition, falls most when people with and without lived experience have contact. **A programme that ignores caste treats effects and leaves the cause in place.**

diagram.caption: poverty and mental illness reinforce each other

key_terms.meaning: Conditions of daily life that shape risk, grouped in five areas by Lund et al.
Debt and money strain, linked to common mental disorders more consistently than income.
Depression in pregnancy and after birth, affecting more than 10% of such women worldwide.
Personal experience of a mental health condition, which should lead stigma reduction.
Laws, insurance exclusions and institutional practices treating mental illness differently.

worked_example.title: Place one case in the five areas
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a livelihoods team notices that a farming family has lost two crops, owes a moneylender and lives in a flood-prone settlement. Use the five-area framework from Lund et al.
steps: Debt and crop loss are economic: livelihoods, social protection, credit.
The flood-prone settlement is environmental events: disaster response, migration support.
Housing and safety are neighbourhood factors.
Choose one entry point the programme controls, such as credit rescheduling, and record it.
worked_example.answer: Economic, environmental and neighbourhood areas all apply, and credit rescheduling is the lever the programme owns.

mistakes: Assuming a larger cash transfer always helps. Financial stress and timeliness matter more than level.
Treating a Dalit student's death as 'personal problems' without asking about caste discrimination.
Collecting no data by social group, so the people left out stay invisible.
Screening only women in clinics and missing men, whose distress shows as alcohol, anger or withdrawal.

recall.q: How many studies did Lund and colleagues review in 2010 and what did they find?
recall.a: 115 studies. 73% of bivariate and 79% of multivariate analyses found a positive association between poverty and common mental disorders.

recall.q: Name the five areas of the Lund 2018 framework.
recall.a: Demographic, economic, neighbourhood, environmental events, and social and cultural.

recall.q: What share of 2024 suicides was recorded as debt-related?
recall.a: 4.4% (bankruptcy or indebtedness).

recall.q: What does the Lancet Commission find works best against stigma?
recall.a: Social contact between people with and without lived experience.

recall.q: How much more common is depression among women, per WHO?
recall.a: About 1.5 times.

sections.title: The law in India: the Mental Healthcare Act and the BNS
sections.big_idea: The 2017 Act gives **rights to care, capacity, community living and confidentiality**, and moved attempted suicide from crime to care.
in_plain_words: The Act replaced the 1987 Act and aligns Indian law with the UN disability convention. It presumes capacity (s4), allows advance directives (s5) and nominated representatives (s14), and makes access to care a right (s18). Section 19 gives a right to community living, s21 equality with physical illness, s95 bans chaining and s99 sets research consent. Admission follows graded routes with safeguards, and emergency treatment is limited to 72 hours.

Section 115 presumes severe stress in an attempt and bars trial under section 309 IPC. The BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, has no general offence of attempted suicide. It keeps abetment offences and one narrow attempt offence aimed at compelling a public servant. In Sukdeb Saha (2025) the Supreme Court held that mental health is part of Article 21. **Read the sections themselves before advising anyone.**

events.what: Mental Health Act on admission and detention

diagram.caption: the legal sequence in six dates

key_terms.meaning: A written statement of how a person wants or does not want to be treated.
An adult a person appoints in writing to support their decisions.
Up to 30 days, with two examinations and the least restrictive option.
Presumes severe stress in an attempt and requires care and rehabilitation.
Attempt with intent to compel or restrain a public servant.

worked_example.title: Which admission route applies?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative cases. Match each to the route in the Act, using the deck's table.
steps: An adult asks to be admitted of their own free will and understands the purpose: independent admission, s86.
A parent applies for a child's admission: s87, with the nominated representative and two independent examinations.
A person at risk of harm to self or others and unable to care for themselves: supported admission, s89, up to 30 days.
Immediate danger to life: emergency treatment, s94, limited to 72 hours or assessment, no ECT.
worked_example.answer: s86, s87, s89 and s94 in that order, each with its own safeguard.

mistakes: Telling someone attempted suicide is still a crime under the BNS. There is no general offence.
Missing the narrow s226 offence, which needs intent to compel or restrain a public servant.
Handling an advance directive casually. Keep a copy only with the person's consent.
Skipping section 99 in a research protocol that includes people with mental illness.

recall.q: Which section makes access to mental healthcare a right?
recall.a: Section 18.

recall.q: What can never be grounds for finding mental illness?
recall.a: Political, economic or social status, caste, religion, or non-conformity with moral, social, cultural or political values (s3(3)).

recall.q: What does s115 presume?
recall.a: That a person who attempts suicide has severe stress, and shall not be tried and punished under the IPC.

recall.q: Which section bans chaining?
recall.a: Section 95, with s95(1)(d) the provision to cite.

recall.q: What did Sukdeb Saha hold?
recall.a: That mental health is an integral part of the right to life under Article 21.

sections.title: India's programmes: from 1982 to Tele-MANAS
sections.big_idea: India has programmes for each step of care, and a development programme's job is to **make the connections work where they break**.
in_plain_words: The National Mental Health Programme began in 1982 and the District Mental Health Programme brought community services to the district level, now covering 767 districts. Ayushman Arogya Mandirs carry mental health in their primary care package. Tele-MANAS has been taking free calls in 20 languages since 10 October 2022. The National Suicide Prevention Strategy aims for a 10% fall in suicide mortality by 2030 against 2020.

Schools have Manodarpan and UMMEED, and the Supreme Court told institutions to use them. Read the care pathway as a chain with six steps from a community worker who notices distress to follow-up in the community. It usually breaks between noticing and first contact, and between district care and return. Funding follows hospitals while need sits in the community, so **ask what a state budget does for the DMHP**.

diagram.caption: the care pathway and where it breaks

key_terms.meaning: District Mental Health Programme, covering 767 districts.
National tele mental health helpline: 14416, free, 24 hours.
India's first National Suicide Prevention Strategy, with the REDS path.
Ministry of Education psychosocial support initiative started 21 July 2020.
The sequence from noticing distress to specialist care and return.

worked_example.title: Turn the NSPS target into a number
worked_example.setup: The strategy aims for a 10% fall by 2030 compared with 2020. Use an index of 100 for 2020 suicide mortality. The index is illustrative.
steps: Set the 2020 baseline at 100.
A 10% fall is 100 × 10 ÷ 100 = 10 index points.
The 2030 target is 100 − 10 = 90.
Check progress against the 2020 baseline, since that is the year the strategy measures from.
worked_example.answer: The 2030 target is 90 on an index where 2020 is 100.

mistakes: Citing the DMHP as functioning because it exists on paper. Posts sanctioned and posts filled are different numbers.
Printing the Tele-MANAS number without testing it in the district's language.
Reading a state's budget line for mental health without splitting hospital and DMHP spending.
Assuming schools need new staff to add mental health. Training teachers to notice and refer comes first.

recall.q: When was Tele-MANAS launched and in how many languages?
recall.a: 10 October 2022, with 20 languages chosen by the states.

recall.q: What does REDS stand for in the NSPS?
recall.a: Reinforce, then the strategy's own word for building health service capacity, then Develop and Strengthen.

recall.q: How many districts does the DMHP cover?
recall.a: 767, per the PIB backgrounder of 7 February 2025.

recall.q: Where does the care pathway usually break?
recall.a: Between notice and first contact, and between district and return.

recall.q: Name two questions to ask of a state budget.
recall.a: Hospital versus DMHP share; whether DMHP funds are released in the first half; whether half-way homes are funded; whether the State Mental Health Authority is funded.

sections.title: Law and programmes across South Asia
sections.big_idea: Colonial-era law is being replaced slowly across the region, and **attempted suicide is treated differently in each country**.
in_plain_words: Bangladesh passed a Mental Health Act in 2018 and still lists attempted suicide in section 309 of its Penal Code. Pakistan omitted section 325 in December 2022, the Federal Shariat Court held the omission repugnant to Islam in May 2026, and an appeal is pending under Article 203D. Nepal has a policy from 1996 and no Mental Health Act, and attempted suicide is no offence there. Sri Lanka still runs on an ordinance with 1873 origins and repealed its attempted suicide offence in 1998.

Rights language usually arrives first in policy and later, if at all, in statute. Without a statute, rights such as consent and review rest on policy, which is easier to change or ignore. Laws in this section were changing during 2026, so **recheck before using it in a policy brief**. WHO counted 20 countries that still criminalise attempted suicide.

key_terms.meaning: Colonial law repealed by Bangladesh in 2018 and replaced in Pakistan in 2001.
Pakistan constitutional rule on how a Shariat Court decision takes effect during an appeal.
2010 change in Pakistan making health a provincial subject.
Sri Lanka's law, whose origins lie in 1873.
Helping or encouraging a suicide, an offence in Nepal under s185.

worked_example.title: Read the Sri Lanka evidence per year
worked_example.setup: Gunnell et al. found 19,769 fewer suicides in 1996-2005 than in 1986-95 after restrictions on the most toxic pesticides. Find the average fall per year.
steps: Count the years in the later period: 1996 to 2005 is 10 years.
Divide the fall by the years: 19,769 ÷ 10 = 1,977.
So about 1,977 fewer suicides per year on average.
Say 'coincided with', as the deck does, because the study is an observation over time.
worked_example.answer: About 1,977 fewer suicides per year, described as a fall that coincided with the restrictions.

mistakes: Advising an NGO in Pakistan without checking the current legal position of section 325.
Telling a Bangladeshi team that India's approach applies there. Bangladesh had not removed its offence as of October 2026.
Citing the Sri Lanka draft bill as law. Treat rights protections as policy commitments until it passes.
Assuming a statute exists in Nepal. It has no dedicated Mental Health Act.

recall.q: Which Bangladeshi law repealed the Lunacy Act 1912?
recall.a: The Mental Health Act, 2018 (Act 60 of 2018).

recall.q: What happened in Pakistan on 18 May 2026?
recall.a: The Federal Shariat Court held the omission of s325 repugnant to Islam and said it stands restored.

recall.q: What does Nepal's s185 punish?
recall.a: Abetment of suicide: up to five years and a fine of up to Rs 50,000.

recall.q: How did Sri Lanka remove the attempt offence?
recall.a: Section 302 of the Penal Code was repealed by Act No. 29 of 1998.

recall.q: How many countries did WHO's 2022 report count as criminalising attempted suicide?

sections.title: Task sharing: the evidence from South Asia and beyond
sections.big_idea: Trained lay workers with supervision can deliver effective treatment, and **trial results hold only when supervision, time and referral exist**.
in_plain_words: Task sharing moves specific, well-defined tasks from specialists to trained non-specialists, with ongoing supervision. It works with a short structured manual, role-play training, weekly supervision, clear referral rules and fidelity checks. It fails when counselling is added to an overloaded worker, training has no supervision or nobody can take referrals.

Six models show the range. Thinking Healthy in Rawalpindi cut maternal depression at 6 months to 23% against 53%. The Healthy Activity Program in Goa had 64% remission against 39%. Counselling for Alcohol Problems helped some men stop. PM+ in Peshawar lowered anxiety and depression, the Friendship Bench in Harare cut symptoms to 13.7% against 49.9% and Atmiyata in Mehsana had an odds ratio of 2.2. **Effect sizes cannot be ranked across them**, because the measures differ.

diagram.caption: six tested models, each with supervision

key_terms.meaning: Moving defined tasks to trained non-specialists with supervision.
Delivering the intervention as designed, checked on recorded sessions.
Randomising whole groups, such as villages or clinics, in place of single people.
PHQ-9 below 10 in HAP, or AUDIT below 8 in CAP.
How much higher the odds of an outcome are: 2.2 for Atmiyata recovery at 3 months.

worked_example.title: How large was the Thinking Healthy effect?
worked_example.setup: At 6 months 23% of intervention mothers and 53% of control mothers had major depression. Express the difference two ways.
steps: Difference in percentage points: 53 − 23 = 30.
Relative fall: 30 ÷ 53 = 57%.
So depression was more than half lower in the intervention group.
Note what did not change: infant weight and height.
worked_example.answer: 30 percentage points, a 57% relative fall, and no difference in infant growth.

mistakes: Adding counselling to an already overloaded worker without time or pay.
Copying a model without checking for supervisors, workers' time and a referral destination.
Reporting only the good result. Thinking Healthy found no change in infant growth and CAP none in daily drinking.
Ranking the six models by their headline numbers. The outcome measures differ.

recall.q: Define task sharing.
recall.a: Moving specific, well-defined tasks from specialists to trained non-specialists who receive ongoing supervision.

recall.q: What did HAP use to enrol and to define remission?
recall.a: PHQ-9 above 14 to enrol, and PHQ-9 below 10 for remission.

recall.q: How many sessions does PM+ have and who delivers them?
recall.a: Five weekly 90-minute sessions delivered by lay health workers.

recall.q: Where was the Friendship Bench trial and who delivered it?
recall.a: Harare, Zimbabwe, by lay health workers, many of them older women.

recall.q: What does a programme need before scaling up?
recall.a: A government partner with a budget line, supervision in a public cadre's job, tested referral to the DMHP and outcomes tracked with a validated measure.

sections.title: Children, work and emergencies
sections.big_idea: Mental health protection reaches schools, workplaces and relief camps, and **the IASC pyramid says all four layers run at the same time**.
in_plain_words: One in seven adolescents lives with a mental disorder. Most protection sits outside clinics: laws, caregiver support, school programmes and safer community and online settings. At work, WHO lists excess workloads, job insecurity, discrimination and harassment as risks. For daily wage earners, mental health at work means timely wages and safe conditions. Staff who hear disclosures need care too, starting with manager training.

In emergencies, almost everyone feels distress and most recover. Start with safety and basic services, and keep counselling for those who need it. The IASC pyramid has four layers, from basic services at the base to specialised care at the top. Psychological first aid, look, listen and link, can be given by any helper after short orientation. **Avoid one-off debriefing and collecting stories you cannot follow up.**

diagram.caption: the IASC pyramid, top layer first

key_terms.meaning: Four layers of support, with basic services as the base.
Humane, supportive, practical help: look, listen, link (WHO 2011).
Mental health and psychosocial support.
Sleep, exercise, problem-solving, interpersonal skills and supportive families.
Care for staff who work with distress, including supervision and leave.

worked_example.title: Place four actions on the pyramid
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: after a cyclone, a team lists four activities. Place each on the correct layer.
steps: Fair and transparent food distribution: layer 1, basic services and security.
Restarting weekly women's group meetings: layer 2, community and family supports.
A trained ASHA running PM+ sessions: layer 3, focused non-specialised supports.
A psychiatrist treating psychosis: layer 4, specialised services.
worked_example.answer: Layers 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively, and all four must be available together.

mistakes: Counselling everyone in an emergency. Restore safety, basic services and community supports first.
Running one-off debriefing sessions or labelling people as traumatised.
Acting as a therapist when giving psychological first aid. Link people to upper layers instead.
Ignoring staff stress while promoting protections for others.

recall.q: What are the three action principles of psychological first aid?
recall.a: Look, listen and link.

recall.q: What share of people who experienced war in the previous ten years has a mental disorder, per WHO?
recall.a: One in five (22%).

recall.q: Name two workplace risks WHO lists.
recall.a: Excessive workloads, long or inflexible hours, low control, job insecurity, inadequate pay, discrimination, violence, harassment or bullying.

recall.q: Which section of the MHCA requires child mental health services?
recall.a: Section 18(4)(e).

recall.q: What does the deck recommend first for staff wellbeing?
recall.a: Manager training so supervisors can recognise distress and respond.

sections.title: Measuring mental health, and researching it ethically
sections.big_idea: Use **validated tools in the local language**, treat a score as a flag, and have a distress protocol before the first interview.
in_plain_words: The PHQ-9 scores depression in nine items from 0 to 3, the GAD-7 measures anxiety and the SRQ-20 screens common mental disorders with yes/no questions. A tool is only as good as its validation in your language. In Goa, positive predictive values were only 51% to 77%, so cut-offs should be set per setting. People often describe distress through the body, so ask about tiredness and 'tension'.

Choose indicators at every level, from mean PHQ-9 change to supervision logs, and measure functioning as well as symptoms. ICMR treats mental illness as a vulnerability that needs safeguards, while saying disorder does not mean incapacity to consent. Write a distress protocol with your ethics committee, treat the data as highly sensitive and **never collect PHQ-9 item 9 without a protocol**.

key_terms.meaning: Nine-item depression scale scored 0 to 3 per item, total 0 to 27.
How many true cases a screening score picks up.
Comparing a tool against a diagnostic interview in the same population.
Pre-agreed steps for enumerators when a respondent is at risk.
The data protection law, with core duties applying from 13 May 2027.

worked_example.title: Score a PHQ-9 and read the band
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a respondent's nine item scores are 2, 1, 3 then 2, 1, 2 then 1, 2, 1.
steps: First three items: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6.
Next three items: 2 + 1 + 2 = 5.
Last three items: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.
Total: 6 + 5 + 4 = 15, which falls in the 15-19 band, moderately severe.
worked_example.answer: A total of 15 is moderately severe. It is a screening flag, so say 'screened positive' and refer.

mistakes: Using a word-for-word translated scale with no validation in the language or population.
Writing 'has depression' on the strength of a screening score alone.
Starting fieldwork on mood or suicide with no distress protocol and no district service map.
Treating the DPDP research exemption as in force now. It applies only from 13 May 2027, and ICMR and MHCA s99 apply today.

recall.q: What are the PHQ-9 severity bands?
recall.a: 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe, 20-27 severe.

recall.q: Why does the SRQ-20 suit low-literacy settings?
recall.a: It has 20 yes/no questions that can be self-administered or read out by an interviewer.

recall.q: What did the Kangra study find about symptoms?
recall.a: Tiredness and body weakness were the most endorsed symptoms.

recall.q: What must consent tell prospective participants under ICMR 6.8.1?
recall.a: How the researcher will respond to suicidal ideation or other risks of harm.

recall.q: Name two rules of thumb for mental health data.
recall.a: Collect only what the analysis needs, separate names from responses, encrypt devices and restrict access, never share lists with officials without consent.

sections.title: A practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: A tested referral pathway, trained staff and a distress protocol help more people than **an ambitious counselling component that collapses**.
in_plain_words: Most practitioners add MHPSS to a livelihoods, education, health or protection programme. Follow six steps: map services, protect (check your core programme adds no stress), train, link, add a structured intervention only if supervision exists, and monitor. A referral pathway is a written agreement on who refers whom, with what information and how the outcome returns. Test every number before launch and offer to accompany a first visit.

Communicate safely about suicide: give help information, share stories of coping and leave out method and location. Use the decision table to match what you notice to what you do. In the illustrative case, a worker asked directly, called a supervisor the same day, and the programme changed its repayment rules. Budget supervision, staff care and travel from the start, and **use the checklist before launch**.

children.label: Two weeks or more, affecting work

key_terms.meaning: Mental health and psychosocial support added to another programme.
A written agreement on who refers whom, to which service and how the outcome returns.
WHO's dos and don'ts for talking and writing about suicide.
A simple agreed set of steps made with the person at risk.
An invented teaching case that describes no real person.

worked_example.title: Use the decision table on Sunita's case
worked_example.setup: The illustrative case: Sunita says she cannot sleep and feels her family would be better off without her. What should the worker do?
steps: Match what the worker notices: talk of not wanting to live, row three of the decision table.
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, in private, and do not promise to keep a risk to life secret.
Make a safety plan and arrange a same-day referral through the supervisor.
Plan the follow-up: Tele-MANAS call with consent, accompanied clinic visit, PHQ-9 repeated at month 3.
worked_example.answer: Ask directly, make a safety plan, refer the same day, and follow up with an accompanied visit.

mistakes: Launching a counselling component with no supervision, no referral destination and no budget for them.
Collecting loan repayments in public with names read out, which adds stress to the people you serve.
Describing the method or location of a suicide in a donor report or social post.
Treating the decision table as a clinical protocol. It is a teaching tool to adapt with a local professional.

recall.q: What are the six steps for integrating MHPSS?
recall.a: Map, protect, train, link, add and monitor.

recall.q: What should a referral pathway record about services?
recall.a: Name, address, days and hours, phone, languages and cost.

recall.q: Name two items from WHO's 'do' list for talking about suicide.
recall.a: Give accurate information on where to seek help, share stories of coping and recovery, educate with facts, take care with bereaved families.

recall.q: Who acts when a participant talks of hopelessness or not wanting to live?
recall.a: A supervisor or counsellor.

recall.q: If you can tick only three checklist boxes, which?
recall.a: The referral pathway, staff training and the distress protocol.

sections.title: Summing up and where next
sections.big_idea: The common thread is the gap between effective care and the people who need it, and **most of that gap sits outside hospitals**.
in_plain_words: The deck closes with eight points. Mental health is well-being, and disorders sit on a continuum with it. In India 10.6% of adults had a current disorder and 70% to 92% were untreated. Recorded suicides are an undercount, and poverty, debt, caste and gender shape risk. On the response side, the MHCA makes care a right and attempted suicide a matter for care, and Tele-MANAS, the DMHP and the NSPS are the public routes.

Trained lay workers with supervision can cut depression sharply, and every programme can notice, respond, refer and avoid harm. Where next: pair this course with Public Health 101 and Social Determinants of Health 101. Take Research Ethics 101 **before any fieldwork that asks about mood or suicide**. If the material was difficult, Tele-MANAS is free and open round the clock.

diagram.caption: the deck's eight points in two groups

key_terms.meaning: Mental health varies by person and over time, shaped at any moment by many factors.
Recorded suicides below the true number.
Section 18 of the MHCA: access to services run or funded by government.
The core action of any programme, with harm avoided.
Courses listed on the last slide for health, methods and determinants.

worked_example.title: Turn the NMHS rate into a village number
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a block has 1,000 adults and the NMHS 10.6% current-disorder rate is applied to it. The deck says the untreated share ranged from 70% to 92% by condition.
steps: Adults with a current disorder: 1,000 × 10.6 ÷ 100 = 106.
If 70% received no treatment: 106 × 0.7 = 74.
If 92% received no treatment: 106 × 0.92 = 97.5.
Say these are rough, because a 12-state survey is being applied to one block.
worked_example.answer: About 106 adults, of whom roughly 74 to 98 would be untreated, as a rough planning guide.

mistakes: Applying a national or 12-state rate to a block and quoting the result as a count of real people.
Reading the summary as a list of laws without checking the country's current position.
Starting fieldwork on mood or suicide before taking a research ethics course.
Forgetting the practitioner's own wellbeing when planning work on this subject.

recall.q: What share of adults had a current mental disorder in NMHS 2015-16?
Which section of the MHCA makes care a right, and which covers attempted suicide?
recall.a: Section 18 for care and section 115 for attempted suicide.

recall.q: Name the three public routes listed in the summary.
recall.a: Tele-MANAS 14416, the DMHP and the NSPS.

recall.q: What did the deck suggest as a course order?
recall.a: Public Health, then Social Determinants of Health, then Research Ethics before fieldwork asking about mood or suicide.

recall.q: Where does most of the gap between care and need sit?
recall.a: Outside hospitals: in villages, schools, workplaces and camps.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a route planner. Sections 1 to 4 describe the problem, 5 to 7 cover law and programmes, 8 and 9 cover what works, and 10 to 12 give you tools. If you work in the field, read **Section 11 first** and return to the evidence afterwards.
notes.4: Hold on to the shift in the first sentence: mental health means well-being, and it can be present in someone with a diagnosis. The two values, intrinsic and instrumental, give you two arguments for any funder. Use the **instrumental argument** when a livelihood or school project wants to claim mental health gains.
notes.5: Three terms form a set of nested circles: disorder is the narrowest, mental health condition the broadest, and psychosocial disability describes the barriers society puts in the way. Match the term to the activity. A **screening survey estimates disorders**, while a community programme works with distress and functioning.
notes.6: ICD-11 is the shared coding language, and section 3(1) of the Act points to it. For you the point is modest: you will not diagnose, but you will read notes and papers written in its terms. Know **where the words come from** so a referral note does not mystify you.
notes.7: Read the definition in section 2(1)(s) as the doorway to every right in the Act. Then read what sits outside it. Intellectual disability is handled under the disability law, and section 3 lists what can never justify a finding of mental illness. Remember **a diagnosis alone does not mean unsound mind**.
notes.8: This table is a working map of conditions, with the global number for each and the treatment WHO names. Read the right-hand column twice. Every row has an effective treatment, so the **central problem is the gap between need and care**. Note the nine-year earlier death for schizophrenia.
notes.9: Compare the two laws by their starting point. The 1987 Act was about admission and detention, while the 2017 Act starts with capacity and choice. Section 4 presumes capacity, and a decision others consider wrong is not proof of incapacity. In practice: **the person decides, and you support**.
notes.10: Use this table as an editing checklist for every report and poster. The reason column is the argument you will need when a colleague objects. The simplest rule is **the person comes before the diagnosis**. Ask people with lived experience what words they use for themselves.
notes.12: Three numbers frame the problem: 1.2 billion people living with a disorder, 1 in 6 years lived with disability and 71% of people with psychosis receiving no service. The money point is as striking: **two in three dollars went to stand-alone hospitals** in place of community services. Section 7 returns to the 20 countries.
notes.13: The care gap is wider than coverage figures suggest, because one prescription and no return visit counts as coverage. The two blocks show the gap widening as incomes fall. Psychosis is treated in about 70% of high-income countries and 12% of low-income ones. Say **which source and year** you quote.
notes.14: Read the five figures together: 197.3 million people with a disorder, roughly equal depression and anxiety counts and a rising share of total DALYs. The range in brackets is an uncertainty interval, so quote it. Remember the final line: **GBD gives scale and comparison, and surveys give programme baselines**.
notes.15: The chart splits the burden by disorder: depression 33.8%, anxiety 19.0%, and schizophrenia plus bipolar disorder 16.7%. The first two account for more than half, which is why primary care and community work target them. The severe disorders are fewer but their **families carry long periods of care**.
notes.16: This slide explains why mhGAP puts mental, neurological and substance use disorders together: the same primary care workers and scarce specialists serve all three. Note the treatment gaps of 86.3% for alcohol and 91.8% for tobacco. Alcohol and drugs are also **inside the Act's own definition**.
notes.17: NMHS 2015-16 is India's only national measurement of prevalence and treatment gap, and it covered 12 states. Keep the four headline numbers in mind: 10.6%, 13.7%, 7.3% and 0.9%. Mind the final box: the survey and GBD **answer different questions**, so never place them in one sentence as if they agree.
notes.18: Treatment gap means the share who got no treatment, and the chart shows it ranges from 70% to 92% by condition. For common disorders it was 85%. The service lesson is the last sentence: **those who did get care mostly used government facilities**, so scale-up must happen in public services.
notes.19: Treat this slide as a rule for dating your sources. NMHS-2 has no published report as of October 2026, so use the 2015-16 survey for national numbers and state the year and the 12 states. Before you quote NMHS-2 in a proposal, **confirm its status** with NIMHANS or the Ministry.
notes.21: Read the content note first: this section follows WHO's guidance of no methods, no locations and help information. The three numbers are 727,000 deaths, third leading cause among those aged 15 to 29, and 73% in low- and middle-income countries. Suicide is rarely a single-cause event, and **the helpline is free all day**.
notes.22: India's NCRB figure is 1,70,746 suicides in 2024, a rate of 12.2 per lakh. Read the state-share line with care. Uttar Pradesh holds 17.0% of the population and reports 5.4% of suicides, and the gap partly reflects **how well each state's police record deaths**. Do not rank states.
notes.23: The chart shows rises from 2020 to 2023 and a levelling in 2024. NCRB uses projected population for non-census years. The 2022 rate of 12.4 was the highest shown. A programme manager should **watch the trend since 2020**, since the National Suicide Prevention Strategy measures its target against that year.
notes.24: The table lists the trigger an officer recorded, with family problems at 33.5% and illness at 17.9%. These are narrow views of a decision with many causes. Use them as **recorded triggers**, and follow WHO's advice never to explain a death with one factor.
notes.25: Daily wage earners were nearly a third of deaths, and housewives were 48.9% of the women who died. Read the figures for the farming sector as two groups: cultivators and agricultural labourers. The pattern points at **insecure work and unpaid domestic work**, where development programmes already operate.
notes.26: Every source of under-count pushes the true figure up, so call the NCRB number a floor. Use the right-hand list as a drill: quote the edition year, compare within one state over time and treat the causes as triggers. Remember that **attempts are not counted** in this series.
notes.27: Each fact in the table has a field consequence. The most useful is the first: asking directly about suicidal thoughts is safe. Learn the six as a set, because they replace the common myths staff bring to the job. WHO's closing point is that **no suicide has a single cause**.
notes.28: Four interventions have the best evidence, and means restriction is the one with a South Asian proof. Sri Lanka's pesticide limits coincided with 19,769 fewer suicides over ten years. The reason it works is stated plainly: **crises are brief**, so time and distance from a means lets the crisis pass.
notes.30: Poverty and mental disorder run in both directions. Read the two boxes as a loop: insecurity and risk push poor people toward illness, and the costs of illness push the household deeper into debt. The review found education the most consistent link and **income alone the weaker one**.
notes.31: The table shows which dimensions of poverty tie to common mental disorders most consistently: education, food, housing, class and financial stress. Income and employment are equivocal. For design, **financial stress matters more than income level**, so a transfer that arrives on time may beat a larger one that arrives late.
notes.32: Five areas, mapped to the SDGs, give a programme team a way to ask where its own work touches mental health. Locate your programme in the 'where programmes act' column. That column is the **deck's own gloss**, so treat it as teaching help and as no part of the review.
notes.33: This slide links the suicide data to rural work. Debt is 4.4% of recorded causes, the farming sector is 6.2% of deaths and daily wage earners are 31.0%. The pressure points are things you can schedule around: repayment dates, crop failure, **wage delays** and migration. Check how payments work under the new law.
notes.34: The research shows gaps for Scheduled Castes and Muslims that status differences did not fully explain. The authors' point is that income support alone will not close them. Remember that a programme ignoring caste **treats the effects while leaving the cause**, so collect data by social group with consent.
notes.35: Depression is about 1.5 times more common among women, and the household is a site of risk in the suicide data. Pair each finding with an action: screening in maternal health, mental health support in violence services, and outreach for men through work sites. Men's distress shows up as **alcohol, anger or withdrawal**.
notes.36: Many people describe stigma as worse than the condition. The Commission's strongest finding is that contact between people with and without lived experience reduces it best. The table sorts stigma into public, self and structural, so ask **which form your programme meets** and who with lived experience is leading.
notes.38: Treat this table as a map of rights and duties by section number. The ones to remember first are s4 capacity, s18 access, s19 community living, s21 parity and s115 attempted suicide. The note at the bottom matters: **read the sections themselves** before advising anyone.
notes.39: Section 18 turns access to care into a legal right and sets a standard: affordable, good quality, close by and without discrimination. Sub-section 4 lists services and sub-section 5 says how to deliver them. Use these as a **yardstick for public services**, and as grounds for a community petition.
notes.40: Three protections here deserve a place in staff training: community living (s19), parity with physical illness including insurance (s21) and the ban on chaining (s95). When you meet chaining at a faith-healing site or home, the provision to cite is **section 95(1)(d)**.
notes.41: Two planning tools let a person decide ahead of a crisis. An advance directive applies only when capacity is lost, and a nominated representative can be named on plain paper. A community programme can help people write one **while they are well**. Keep a copy only with consent.
notes.42: The table shows four routes into hospital with different safeguards. For emergency treatment, remember the limits: prevent harm only, 72 hours at most, no ECT. Supported admission is an exception, and section 18(5)(c) puts **community treatment first**. Know which route a person you accompany is on.
notes.43: Section 115 changed attempted suicide from a matter for police to a matter for care: severe stress is presumed, and government must provide care. The history box shows how the courts moved. Its practical effect is that **emergency staff can treat first** without fearing a police case.
notes.44: The BNS has no general attempt offence, so the duty of care in s115(2) is what matters in practice. The three sections left concern abetment and one narrow protest-related attempt. Read s226 carefully: it needs **intent to compel or restrain a public servant**, so distress alone falls outside it.
notes.45: In Sukdeb Saha, the Supreme Court held that mental health is part of Article 21 and set guidelines for institutions. Keep the table's four rows as a policy checklist for any school or coaching centre. The two most concrete: a trained counsellor at 100 or more students and **no public shaming or batch segregation**.
notes.46: Two provisions affect development staff differently. Section 100 gives police a duty of care toward homeless people in crisis, and section 99 sets consent rules for research. If you evaluate programmes, put **section 99 into your protocol** along with ICMR. Section 23 confidentiality applies to your records too.
notes.48: NMHP started in 1982 and the DMHP brought services to the district. Treat the 'falls short' list as a field checklist. Then ask the district three questions: is the psychiatrist post filled, which days does the team visit, and **which medicines are in stock this month**?
notes.49: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs carry mental health in their primary care package, and they are where most rural people first meet the health system. The workforce numbers show scale, but your lever is the home-visiting worker. Teach ASHAs and anganwadi workers to **notice and refer** on visits that already happen.
notes.50: Tele-MANAS is a 24-hour, free service in 20 languages. Three practical rules close the slide: print the number on everything, test it in your district's language and record referrals with consent. A helpline is worth only as much as the **follow-up you build around it**.
notes.51: The strategy sets one target: a 10% fall in suicide mortality by 2030 against 2020. REDS is a memory aid for its four aims: reinforce, build service capacity, develop and strengthen. The timeline gives you milestones at 3, 5 and 8 years to **check state progress against**.
notes.52: School programmes appear at three levels: Manodarpan's support, UMMEED's guidelines and the Supreme Court's direction to use them. WHO rates school social and emotional learning as especially effective. Education programmes can add mental health **without new staff** by training teachers to notice and refer.
notes.53: Walk the six steps as a journey one villager might take. The question for your programme is where it breaks. The slide names two weak points: notice-to-first-contact (shame, travel cost) and district-to-return (no follow-up). **Accompaniment and a named contact** fix both.
notes.54: Two facts pull apart: two thirds of money goes to hospitals, while the Act calls institutions a last resort. Use the table as a budget reading list. The first question, hospitals versus DMHP, tells you whether **money follows the community mandate**. Pair this with the Public Finance course.
notes.56: Bangladesh has a 2018 Mental Health Act, and the Penal Code still lists attempted suicide. For programmes, the criminal provision makes families avoid hospitals after an attempt. Write clear **confidentiality protocols** for staff. The shared Penal Code ancestry with India explains why the comparison is useful.
notes.57: Pakistan's position changed twice in 2026, so read the timeline in order: omission in 2022, restoration by the Federal Shariat Court in May 2026 and an appeal in June. Under Article 203D an appeal can hold the decision. The deck says to **check the current position before advising** any programme.
notes.58: Nepal has had a policy since 1996 and no Mental Health Act. Without a statute, consent, review of admissions and insurance parity rest on policy, which is easier to ignore. Nepal's training of existing health workers resembles Indian approaches. Attempted suicide is no offence, and **abetment is punished**.
notes.59: Sri Lanka runs on an ordinance with origins in 1873, with a new bill in consultation. Its pesticide evidence is the strongest regional case for regulation as prevention. Attempted suicide ceased to be an offence in 1998. Until a law passes, treat rights as **policy commitments**.
notes.60: Read across each row for attempted suicide, because that column shows the biggest differences. India and Nepal have no general offence, Bangladesh still lists section 309, Pakistan is contested and Sri Lanka repealed in 1998. The warning at the foot applies: **laws were changing in 2026**, so recheck.
notes.62: Task sharing moves defined tasks to trained non-specialists with supervision, and specialists keep complex cases. The 'works' and 'fails' lists are your design checklist. Most failures are about **overloading a worker** or training without supervision. Remember the key ingredient: someone to refer to.
notes.63: Thinking Healthy is the anchor trial: lady health workers delivered a CBT-based programme to depressed mothers. Depression at 6 months was 23% against 53%, and at 12 months 27% against 59%. The detail to keep is that **infant weight and height did not differ**, and the slide reports it.
notes.64: HAP used behavioural activation in Goa's primary health centres with lay counsellors. Remission at 3 months was 64% against 39%, and it was cost-effective with an 87% chance. HAP also reduced disability, suicidal thoughts or attempts and partner violence. **PHQ-9 defines both entry and remission** here.
notes.65: CAP targeted harmful drinking in men, a neglected part of mental health in South Asia. More men reached remission (36% against 26%), and 42% against 18% were abstinent. The mixed result matters: daily consumption did not fall among men who kept drinking, so plan **follow-up and family support**.
notes.66: PM+ has four components and five weekly 90-minute sessions delivered by lay health workers. After 3 months, anxiety scores were lower by 2.77 points and depression by 2.98. The table is a ready teaching list of the **four skills** that the sessions teach.
notes.67: The Friendship Bench shows the model outside South Asia: six problem-solving sessions on a clinic bench, with depression symptoms at 13.7% against 49.9%. The three lessons at the bottom transfer: screen with a **locally validated tool**, hold sessions where people go and choose counsellors the community trusts.
notes.68: Atmiyata used village volunteers in 645 Mehsana villages in a stepped-wedge trial. Odds ratios of 2.2 at 3 months and 3.0 at 8 months describe recovery. Its link to welfare entitlements means it **uses the same village structures** as livelihood and social protection programmes.
notes.69: This table lines up six models, and its warning is the main lesson: the outcome measures differ, so you cannot rank effect sizes across rows. What all six share is a comparison group, a manual, supervision and a route to psychiatric care. Check that **your setting has what the trial had**.
notes.70: A trial shows what works under supervision and funding, and routine services rarely have either. Use the two lists as a pre-scaling audit. The strongest sign of readiness is a **budget line and a supervisory role inside a public cadre**. Impact Evaluation 101 covers retesting in a new setting.
notes.72: One in seven adolescents lives with a mental disorder. The risks include violence, bullying and harsh parenting, while protective factors include sleep, exercise and supportive families. NCRB lists exam failure among causes for children under 18. Both the risk list and the protective list give **programmes something to act on**.
notes.73: Most protection for young people lies outside clinics. Use the table as a checklist by setting: early childhood, school, coaching centres and hostels, child protection and online. Section 18(4)(e) requires child services, and section 87 restricts admission of a minor. Cross-read with **Child Rights 101** and SEL Basics 101.
notes.74: Work is an exposure and a protector. The three WHO numbers give the cost, and the risk list gives the causes. Since most South Asian workers have no employer policy, mental health at work means **timely wages, safe conditions and freedom from harassment**. Work, Labour & Livelihoods 101 covers the Codes.
notes.75: Staff who hear disclosures of violence, debt and grief carry risk themselves. Use the left list for early warning in your team and the right list for what your organisation owes. WHO recommends **manager training** so supervisors can recognise distress, and the deck says to start there.
notes.76: Almost everyone in an emergency feels distress, and most recover, so counselling everyone is the wrong first move. The practical order is safety, basic services and community supports. Then specialised care for the minority who need it. The IASC and NDMA guidelines are your **reference documents**.
notes.77: Read the pyramid from the base up. Everyone needs basic services and security, and fewer people need each layer above. All four layers must run **at the same time**. The two bottom boxes show what to do and what to avoid: look, listen and link, and skip one-off debriefing.
notes.78: Psychological first aid is look, listen, link. Learn the three as steps you could teach in an orientation, since any helper can give it. The 'what it avoids' box matters equally: no pressing for stories, no false promises, no acting as a therapist. **Link people to the upper layers** when they need more.
notes.80: The PHQ-9 has nine items scored 0 to 3, with bands from mild to severe. A score of 10 or more had 88% sensitivity and specificity in the original study. Item 9 asks about self-harm, so **never collect it without a pre-agreed response** ready for any positive answer.
notes.81: Each tool has a job. PHQ-9 tracks depression, GAD-7 tracks anxiety and SRQ-20 screens more broadly with a yes/no format that suits low literacy. Learn the closing rule: a screening score is a flag. Write **'screened positive'** in reports and 'has depression' only after clinical assessment.
notes.82: A translated questionnaire can miss how distress is expressed locally, such as tiredness or 'tension'. The Goa study found positive predictive values of only 51% to 77%, so set cut-offs for each setting. The Hindi study in Kangra shows the work involved. **Search for a validation** in your language first.
notes.83: Scales count symptoms that clinicians defined, and people describe distress in their own words. Use the left list as a sequence of groundwork before any survey. The Kangra finding is the lesson: **tiredness and body weakness** were the most endorsed symptoms, so ask about them. Qualitative Methods 101 shows how.
notes.84: The slide separates outputs from outcomes. Counting people trained or sessions held is an output. The table gives indicators at each level, from PHQ-9 change to supervision logs, each disaggregated. The closing advice is practical: **measure functioning as well as symptoms**, since people judge recovery by whether they can work and care.
notes.85: ICMR treats mental illness as a vulnerability needing safeguards and says vulnerable groups have a right to be included. The quotation in the middle is useful for ethics committees: a disorder does not equal incapacity to consent. Section 6.8.1 adds that consent must **explain the response to suicidal ideation**.
notes.86: Write the six-step protocol with your ethics committee before fieldwork. The order protects both people: pause, ask about safety, offer Tele-MANAS and a named local service, stay if risk is immediate, refer through the supervisor, and debrief the enumerator. **Asking does not cause harm**, and WHO lists the opposite as a myth.
notes.87: Mental health data are very sensitive. Section 23 of the Act already gives confidentiality, and the DPDP duties take effect from 13 May 2027, so treat them as the standard to prepare for. Remember the research exemption has conditions and **is not in force before that date**. ICMR and section 99 apply now.
notes.89: Most practitioners add MHPSS to another programme. Walk the six steps in order: map, protect, train, link, add and monitor. The second step is easily skipped: **check that your core programme adds no stress**. Budget supervision, staff care and referral travel from the start.
notes.90: A referral pathway is a written agreement, and the table lists what it needs, from services to review. Do the test before launch: call each service and visit the nearest. Fear of being seen and travel cost are the top barriers, so **offer to accompany** a first visit.
notes.91: Everything you publish counts as public communication. Check each draft against the do and don't lists. Lead with stories of coping and recovery, since WHO reports that widely shared suicide stories are followed by more suicides. The don't list includes **method, location, notes and single-cause explanations**.
notes.92: This is a decision table for field staff, and the deck says to adapt it with a local professional. Read down the rows as rising urgency: low mood, two weeks or more, hopelessness, immediate risk. At the top level the rule is **stay with the person** and call 112 or the nearest hospital and Tele-MANAS.
notes.93: This case is invented, and the deck labels it so. Look at it in two columns: what the worker did well, and what the programme got wrong. Public repayment collection with names read aloud is the stressor. The lesson is that **the core programme can add stress** while one trained worker can reduce risk.
notes.94: Follow the timeline from same-day safety to a repeat PHQ-9 at month 3. The same-day supervisor visit and the consented call to Tele-MANAS are the turning points. Then read the programme changes: private repayments, a hardship rule and referral sheets. **The programme changed its own rules**, which made it work.
notes.95: This is a sample agenda for a one-day orientation, adapted with a local professional. The methods column favours practice: role-play, practice calls and case vignettes. The final paragraph is the design rule: **follow training with monthly supervision**, because training alone fades within weeks.
notes.96: Use the two-column checklist before launch. Design items cover services, referral, stress in the core programme, lived experience and budget. Delivery items cover training, protocol, tools, data and messaging. If you can tick only three, choose **referral pathway, staff training and distress protocol**.
notes.98: Eight points sort into the problem and the response. Test yourself: can you say each in one sentence with its figure? The line to remember is the common thread, the gap between effective care and people in need, most of which sits **outside hospitals**. Tele-MANAS is free, round the clock.
notes.99: Use this page to choose your next course. The suggested order is Public Health, then Social Determinants of Health, then Research Ethics, and the third comes **before any fieldwork** that asks about mood or suicide. Methods courses cover questionnaires, impact evaluation, safeguarding and data protection.
